The proposal offers a genuinely integrated, regulation-aware causal-AI research programme with a well-articulated four-pillar structure, concrete training events, and a structured supervisory governance model (ITP/PCDP/Supervisory Board), which together address the criterion very well. However, 'beyond SOTA' claims and several KPIs (e.g., clinician confidence ratings, workshop participant counts) remain assertions or soft metrics without comparator baselines, methodological depth on causal identifiability is schematic, and supervisor seniority/track record is uneven across the consortium, keeping the proposal short of excellent on soundness and supervision depth.

The proposal presents an ambitious, well-structured four-pillar research programme with nine complementary DC projects, a regulatory-integrated methodology, and a detailed triple-i training and layered supervision architecture (Sections 1.1-1.4), which together address all four aspects substantively. However, recurring reliance on count-based KPIs rather than outcome baselines, under-specified causal-methodological detail, unclear supervisor-to-DC mapping, and an unsubstantiated claim of joint-doctorate-equivalent supervision quality constitute a moderate but real set of shortcomings, placing the work in the 'very good' rather than 'excellent' band.

The proposal addresses all four Excellence aspects with a coherent, ambitious four-pillar framework, concrete KPIs, a detailed and credible training programme (1.3) with named events mapped to TG1-TG6, and a supervision structure with quantified track records and governance procedures (1.4). However, the methodology (1.2) stays largely at a programmatic level without naming specific causal-inference or federated-learning techniques, the nine DC descriptions are heavily templated reducing individual depth, and the joint-supervision quality claim is asserted rather than evidenced, together constituting a small number of non-trivial shortcomings consistent with a 'Very Good' rather than 'Excellent' rating.

The section presents a comprehensive, well-integrated four-pillar programme with concrete KPIs, nine clearly specified DC projects, a detailed triple-i training schedule, and a governance-rich supervision model (ITP, PCDP, Supervisory Board, escalation procedure), which together address all four aspects well. However, ambition claims rely on narrative assertion rather than quantified baselines or named competing methods, several KPIs are soft/process-oriented, and the supervisor-profile table is uneven and partly incomplete, preventing a top score. These are a small number of addressable shortcomings against a strong overall structure, placing the criterion at the upper end of 'Very Good'.

The proposal presents an ambitious, well-integrated four-pillar programme with timely regulatory embedding and a clearly governed supervision/training architecture (Sections 1.3.3–1.3.4, 1.4.2), which supports a Very-Good-leaning score. However, the DC objective blocks are templated and the methodology (Section 1.2) remains conceptual without concrete causal-technical specification, KPIs rely on small samples, and supervisor quality is only assessable through anonymised profile tables, producing a consistent set of shortcomings across all four aspects that prevent an Excellent rating.

Aspects 2.1 and 2.2 are addressed with concrete, quantified measures (secondment targets, PCDP/PhD-committee structure, sustainability hub) that substantiate credibility, but the ≥80% non-academic secondment claim conflicts with the DC table data in the appendix. Aspects 2.3 and 2.4 are present but largely generic: the dissemination/communication plan under-specifies non-scientific communication activities, and the magnitude/importance of impacts in 2.4 is asserted without quantification. The mix of two strong and two moderately weak aspects, plus an internal data inconsistency, places the proposal at 'Good' with a number of shortcomings rather than 'Very Good'.

The structuring and career-development aspects (2.1, 2.2) are addressed very well with concrete mechanisms, measurable targets, and governance structures, but the appendix DC table reveals the headline 'non-academic sector' secondment statistic is not actually met, weakening that claim's credibility. The dissemination/exploitation (2.3) and magnitude-of-impact (2.4) aspects are present but rely heavily on generic, unquantified language (e.g., 'improved model robustness', 'improved diagnostic accuracy') without baseline comparators or concrete communication KPIs distinct from publication counts, consistent with the harness's non-passing assessment of those two aspects. Taken together the section addresses all four aspects but with a number of shortcomings, placing it solidly in the 'Good' band with some movement toward 'Very Good' given the strength of the training/career elements.

The structuring/training (2.1) and career-development (2.2) aspects are addressed with concrete, measurable commitments (secondment quotas, PCDP/PhD-committee design, Academy/alumni sustainability mechanisms), but the dissemination/exploitation (2.3) and magnitude-of-impact (2.4) aspects rely heavily on generic boilerplate and unquantified claims ('improved diagnostic accuracy', 'reduce delays in care', standard IP-management language) without baselines, metrics or audience-specific communication detail. This mixed profile—strong on two aspects, noticeably thinner on the other two—places the proposal solidly in the 'good with a number of shortcomings' band rather than very good.

Together these shortcomings in two of the four aspects, despite real strengths in the other two, place the proposal at 'Good' rather than 'Very Good'.

However, the dissemination/communication plan (2.3) stays largely generic on audience segmentation and metrics, and the magnitude-of-impact aspect (2.4) relies on qualitative assertions ('improved robustness', 'strengthen competitiveness') without quantified scale, bringing the holistic score down to the Good/Very-Good boundary.

The work plan is thorough and traceable, with well-specified WPs/tasks, a deliverables/milestones table, and a risk register linking mitigations to specific WPs, and Section 3.2 credibly maps infrastructure and expertise complementarities across beneficiaries and associated partners. However, the absence of any person-month/effort quantification for work packages or participants, limited technical-risk methodology, an unaddressed WP2/WP4 task overlap, and generic (non-evidenced) participant capacity descriptions constitute a moderate cluster of shortcomings consistent with a 'very good with some shortcomings' rating rather than excellent.

These gaps prevent a 'Very Good' or higher rating despite the clear logical coherence and completeness of the deliverable/milestone/risk machinery. The work plan (Section 3.1) is detailed and well-structured with tasks, deliverables, milestones and a reasonably thorough risk table, but lacks an explicit effort/PM allocation or dependency mapping, leaving 'appropriateness of effort' only implicitly supported by participant lists. The participants section (3.2) and Section 8 profiles tie infrastructure to WPs convincingly, yet the organisation descriptions remain generic and sanitised, offering limited concrete evidence of individual capacity beyond facility lists. These combined strengths and gaps place the criterion solidly in the 'Very Good' band with a small number of real shortcomings rather than 'Excellent'.

The work-plan narrative (WPs 1-7, deliverables/milestones/risk tables) and the participant-capacity narrative (infrastructure-to-WP mapping, complementarity argument, associated-partner roles) together address both aspects with clear structure and reasonable detail, warranting a 'Very Good' tier score. However, the complete absence of any person-month/effort distribution table across WPs or tasks is a substantive gap against the explicit 'appropriateness of effort assigned to work packages' aspect, and risk mitigations are at times generic, which together constitute more than a minor shortcoming and keep the score just below the 4.0 threshold.

The section provides a thorough, well-cross-referenced work plan (WP1-7, deliverables, milestones, risks) and a clear mapping of participant infrastructure and complementary expertise to tasks, which supports a 'good to very good' rating, but the absence of any effort/person-month quantification and the reliance on generic capacity descriptors rather than evidenced track records introduce multiple shortcomings that keep the score below 'very good'. The risk table's heavy skew toward recruitment/administrative issues over scientific-technical risks in WP1-3 is a further gap an applicant could readily remedy.
